coNbc: For new houses, the National Building Code 2020 (Article 9.32.3.9) requires a CO alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door when the home has a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage, an alarm in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance (on or near the ceiling unless the maker's instructions say otherwise), and interconnected alarms in a house with a secondary suite.

co.text: B.C. doesn't require CO alarms in existing homes; the province recommends them wherever there's a fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage, and the building code requires them in new homes.
install: Not required in existing homes; the province recommends alarms wherever there's a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage.
New homes served by or containing a fuel-burning appliance, or with an attached garage, need CO alarms under the BC Building Code.

wells.text: There's no free provincial program: use a qualified lab (search the CALA directory), which supplies the bottles. HealthLinkBC recommends testing for bacteria at least once a year and for chemistry when the well is new and annually after that.

co.text: Alberta requires CO alarms in new homes with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage; for existing homes the province calls them highly recommended rather than mandatory.
install: Required in new homes with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage; for existing homes the province calls them highly recommended.
Alberta's fire code requires CO alarms that are installed to be inspected, tested and maintained following the manufacturer's instructions.

wells.text: Alberta Health Services tests private well water free, for bacteria plus chemistry and trace metals; pick up bottles at AHS facilities. Test for bacteria twice a year and for chemistry every three years.

co.text: Saskatchewan requires CO alarms in all residential buildings regardless of age (enforced since July 1, 2022), and from November 1, 2026, 'Henry's Law' requires one in every residential suite, including secondary suites.
install: Required in all residential buildings, whatever their age, that contain a fuel-burning appliance, an attached garage or more than one suite (enforced since July 1, 2022).
In a house, put an alarm inside each bedroom or within 5 m outside each bedroom door, plus one in any room with a solid-fuel-burning appliance such as a wood stove.
From November 1, 2026, Henry's Law requires a CO alarm in every residential suite, including houses with secondary suites.

wells.text: The Roy Romanow Provincial Laboratory tests well water for a fee: $23 for bacteria and $29 for a potability panel in its published schedule (confirm current prices). Bottles are at rural municipality and public health offices. Test yearly for bacteria and nitrate.

co.text: Manitoba's Fire Code requires CO detection only in buildings subject to fire-safety inspections, not in ordinary private homes, so installing alarms is up to you.
install: The Manitoba Fire Code requires CO detection only in buildings that need regular fire-safety inspections, such as care homes, schools and hotels; private houses aren't on the list.

wells.text: Manitoba's Private Well Testing Subsidy covers one bacteria test a year for $17.67 at Duracan Laboratory in Winnipeg, with a free re-test after a positive result. Test at least once a year, ideally after snowmelt.

co.text: Ontario's Fire Code requires CO alarms in existing homes that have a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage: next to every sleeping area and, since January 1, 2026, on every storey as well.
install: Required in every home with a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage, and since January 1, 2026 also in homes served by a forced-air fuel-burning appliance located outside the building.
Put an alarm next to each sleeping area and, since January 1, 2026, on every storey that has no sleeping area.
Hardwired, battery and plug-in alarms are all allowed.
The homeowner is responsible in an owner-occupied home, and the landlord in a rental.

wells.text: Free bacteria testing through Public Health Ontario labs: pick up a kit at a PHO lab or your public health unit and drop it back off. Chemistry (nitrate, sodium, metals) goes to a licensed private lab for a fee. Local health units recommend testing at least three times a year: spring, summer and fall.

co.text: Quebec has no province-wide rule requiring CO alarms in existing houses: provincial rules cover larger multi-unit buildings, and for houses it's up to each municipality's by-law, so ask your local fire service.
install: There's no province-wide rule for houses: municipal by-laws decide, so ask your municipal fire service.

Provincial rules cover larger buildings (multi-unit buildings of more than 2 storeys and 8 units, rooming houses, hotels and seniors' residences), where units with a combustion appliance or direct access to an indoor parking garage need a CO alarm.

wells.text: There's no free provincial service: send samples to a lab accredited by Quebec's environment ministry (the CEAEQ list), which supplies the bottles. The ministry recommends testing for bacteria at least twice a year, in spring and fall, plus a chemical analysis while the well is in use.

co.text: We found no New Brunswick rule requiring CO alarms in existing homes; new construction follows the 2020 National Building Code.
install: We found no provincial rule requiring CO alarms in existing homes; new construction follows the 2020 National Building Code.

wells.text: Owners pay: test kits are at Service New Brunswick offices or RPC, the designated provincial lab in Fredericton and Moncton. The province recommends testing for bacteria twice a year and for inorganic contaminants every two years.

co.text: Nova Scotia's building code requires CO alarms in new homes with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage, but older homes don't have to be retrofitted; the province recommends them.
install: New homes with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage need a CO alarm under the building code; older homes don't have to be retrofitted unless a building official or fire inspector orders it.
Nova Scotia's fire safety rules require CO alarms to be inspected, tested and maintained following the manufacturer's instructions.

wells.text: Owners pay: Nova Scotia Health charges $34.50 for a bacteria test and $37.63 to $138.77 for chemical packages, with bottles at NSH locations. The province recommends testing for bacteria every year and for chemicals every five years.

co.text: PEI's Fire Marshal advises CO alarms outside each sleeping area and on every level, but we found no rule requiring them in existing homes.
install: We found no rule requiring CO alarms in existing homes; PEI's Fire Marshal advises installing them outside each sleeping area and on every level.

wells.text: Free since January 1, 2022: bacteria and general chemistry for residential wells through PEI Analytical Laboratories, with bottles at the lab or any Access PEI site. Test for bacteria yearly and chemistry every two years.

co.text: Newfoundland and Labrador's fire regulations require smoke alarms in existing homes but contain no CO alarm requirement.
install: The province's fire regulations require smoke alarms in existing homes but contain no CO alarm requirement.

wells.text: Free bacteria testing: sterile bottles are at Government Service Centres and the NL Public Health Laboratory. Chemistry goes to an approved private lab for a fee.

co.text: Yukon requires CO detectors in every residence with a fuel-burning appliance or attached garage.
install: Every Yukon residence with a fuel-burning appliance or an attached garage must have CO detectors (Government of Yukon).

wells.text: Free bacteria testing at Yukon's Environmental Health Services water lab in Whitehorse (867-667-8391). No Yukon lab tests chemistry, so those samples go to accredited labs in B.C. or Alberta, often around $200 plus shipping.

co.text: We found no NWT requirement for CO alarms in existing homes; the territory's fire regulations adopt the national codes for new construction.
install: We found no territorial requirement for existing homes; the NWT applies the 2020 National Building Code to new construction.

wells.text: There's no free program: the GNWT's Taiga Environmental Laboratory in Yellowknife tests private samples ($28 for bacteria in its 2021 price guide) and supplies bottles free.
